learn.intro: Who gained and who lost from European expansion? This topic brings the unit together, introduces the transatlantic slave trade as a direct consequence of what you have studied, and asks who deserves to be remembered as a significant traveller, ready for your AP1 research project.

sections.title: 1. Who gained and who lost?

blocks.p: European expansion after 1492 had very different consequences for different groups:

ul: EUROPEAN POWERS gained enormously: silver and gold from the Americas (especially from Spanish mines at Potosí, from 1545), new crops and new colonies.
INDIGENOUS AMERICANS faced catastrophe: population collapse from disease, loss of land and independence, forced labour and conquest. They also survived, resisted and kept their cultures alive.

ENSLAVED AFRICANS: as Indigenous populations collapsed and European demand for labour on sugar plantations grew, Europeans turned to the forced transportation of enslaved people from West and Central Africa across the Atlantic. Over more than 300 years, over 12 million Africans were forcibly transported.

blocks.p: The transatlantic slave trade was directly connected to the processes you have studied: the Columbian Exchange, colonisation and plantation sugar.

"Winners and losers" can oversimplify. Not all Europeans gained (many ordinary sailors and soldiers died or gained little), and Indigenous and African peoples were not passive victims: they resisted, adapted and shaped outcomes.

evidence: Over 12 million Africans were forcibly transported across the Atlantic over more than 300 years.

sections.title: 2. Who changed the world? Judging significance

blocks.p: Significance is judged with criteria, not popularity: scale, impact, duration, revealing and remembered (the same toolkit you used in Year 7).

The criteria give surprising results. Zheng He's voyages were arguably larger in scale than Columbus's, but had less lasting global impact because China ended them. Columbus's first voyage was smaller, but its consequences, the Columbian Exchange and colonisation, were transformative and irreversible.
Significance also depends on whose perspective you take and which criteria you prioritise.

evidence: Criteria: scale, impact, duration, revealing, remembered.

sections.title: 3. Ready to research: your AP1 project

blocks.p: For AP1 you research one traveller or explorer and answer: How significant was your traveller's journey, and how should they be remembered?

Your planning sheet needs: the traveller and dates; your central argument; at least three credible sources with a bibliography; evidence about the route; motives; encounters; consequences; your chosen significance criteria; at least one alternative perspective; and an initial judgement.
Use credible sources (museums, universities, published historians) and record where each fact comes from.

evidence.q: Explain how the transatlantic slave trade was connected to earlier events in this unit.
evidence.model: Disease collapsed Indigenous populations, while the Columbian Exchange brought sugar to the Americas. Europeans then forcibly transported enslaved Africans to work on sugar plantations.

evidence.q: Use two criteria to compare the significance of Zheng He and Columbus.
evidence.model: Zheng He scores highly on scale, with seven huge expeditions, but lower on duration because China ended them. Columbus's voyage was smaller in scale, but its impact and duration were enormous because it began the Columbian Exchange and colonisation.

sources.label: Source A
sources.provenance: Data from the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database (SlaveVoyages), built by an international team of historians from shipping records since the 1990s.
sources.text: The database records tens of thousands of slave-trading voyages. Its estimates show that over 12 million Africans were forced onto ships across the Atlantic between the 1500s and 1800s, and that well over a million died during the crossing. It also lists the ships, their owners and the European and American ports they sailed from.

questions.sources_note: Source A is described in our own words for revision practice. In the exam you will be given the source itself.

questions.label: Teacher-created practice question
questions.q: "Everyone involved in European expansion was either a winner or a loser." How far do you agree?
questions.asks: Test the winners/losers model against the evidence for each group.
steps: Show who clearly gained or lost.
Show where the model oversimplifies (ordinary Europeans; resistance).
questions.plan: 2 minutes planning, 9 minutes writing, 1 minute checking.
mistakes: Treating Indigenous and African people as passive

full: P: I agree to some extent because…

some: P – Topic sentence with a qualifier (blue): One key reason … / To a large extent … / On the other hand …
E – Precisely selected evidence (purple), in order with time connectives (green): At the start … / Later … / Eventually … / Finally …
E – Explain with arguing connectives (red): However … / This was more important because … / In contrast …
J – Judgement: This shows that … / Overall, the most important reason was … / Therefore, I agree to a large/limited extent …
